subject: Archaeology
title: Radiocarbon Dating Explained
description: A micro-lesson that makes Radiocarbon Dating Explained usable.

hook.text: Every living thing absorbs a radioactive form of carbon. When it dies, that carbon starts ticking like a clock.

buildup.text: Carbon-14 decays at a known rate — half of it disappears every 5,730 years. Measuring what is left reveals the age.

discovery.text: Willard Libby invented the technique in 1949 and won the Nobel Prize. It revolutionized archaeology overnight.

twist.text: It only works on organic material — bone, wood, charcoal, and shells. Stones and metals cannot be radiocarbon dated.

climax.text: Modern accelerator mass spectrometry can date a single grain of wheat and needs samples thousands of times smaller.

punchline.text: A ticking atomic clock hides inside every bone and seed.

quiz.question: What is the half-life of Carbon-14?

details.summary: Radiocarbon dating measures the decay of carbon-14 in organic materials to determine their age. Living organisms absorb carbon-14 from the atmosphere; after death, it decays at a known rate. This allows dating of wood, bone, shell, and charcoal up to about 50,000 years old.
details.whyItMatters: Radiocarbon dating revolutionized archaeology by providing absolute dates for organic materials worldwide. Before its invention in 1949, archaeologists relied on relative dating methods that could not produce calendar age estimates.
takeaways: Measures carbon-14 decay in organic materials after death
Effective for materials up to approximately 50,000 years old
Revolutionized archaeology by providing absolute calendar dates

faq.question: How accurate is radiocarbon dating?
faq.answer: Modern accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) dating typically produces results accurate to within 20-50 years for samples under 10,000 years old. Calibration against tree-ring chronologies corrects for variations in atmospheric carbon-14 levels, improving accuracy significantly.

faq.question: Why can't radiocarbon dating work on very old materials?
faq.answer: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years. After about 50,000 years, so little remains that it becomes unmeasurable. For older materials, archaeologists use potassium-argon dating, uranium series dating, or other methods suited to geological timescales.
